title: Racing Engineering wins Le Castellet on ELMS debut
dek: Racing Engineering's Oreca #24 won the 4 Hours of Le Castellet on its debut, Pla passing Alpine's Thiriet for the lead and finishing 4.827 seconds clear after DragonSpeed's crash.

chapters.title: A new-look LMP2 field arrives at Paul Ricard
text: The 2018 European Le Mans Series opened with the 4 Hours of Le Castellet on 15 April, and the paddock arrived after a week of the wrong kind of weather: gale-force winds on the first Sunday, then rain and hail that left only two of the five Prologue sessions properly dry. Paul Ricard had been resurfaced, pit lane included, since the previous summer's race, which had also been run with a chicane on the Mistral Straight, so last year's times were of little use. The grid was huge, 45 cars in all with 19 of them in LMP2, and the top class was full of newcomers.

Racing Engineering, a long-time single-seater outfit, was making its sportscar debut with an ex-Rebellion Oreca 07 in Spanish colours. IDEC Sport, the reigning champions, had swapped a planned second Ligier for a brand-new Oreca that only reached the team a week before the race. Algarve Pro Racing added an ex-Manor Oreca to its Ligier, and SMP Racing unveiled a new Dallara. The test had been topped by 21-year-old Henrique Chaves, a sports car rookie, whose 1:41.018 for AVF's Dallara on Monday evening was the fastest lap of the week.

TDS Racing came across from the World Endurance Championship as a guest entry, running as #33 because IDEC was using the #28 the team carries in the WEC. Loïc Duval, absent from the test because of DTM commitments, joined Perrodo and Vaxiviere, and the trio planned to contest the first three ELMS rounds. Signatech Alpine also arrived from the WEC paddock, while G-Drive Racing was without Jean-Eric Vergne, who was racing in Formula E in Rome, so Imperatori completed its line-up.

chapters.title: Chatin puts IDEC on a maiden pole
text: Qualifying lasted only ten minutes and was split in two when Bruno Senna stopped the #22 Ligier on the Mistral Straight and brought out the red flags. Paul-Loup Chatin had already gone fastest with a 1:41.523 and, once the session resumed, he found more, taking the new #28 Oreca to pole with a 1:41.194, the first in IDEC Sport's ELMS history. Team-mate Memo Rojas said the crew had only received the car a week earlier.

Matthieu Vaxiviere put the TDS Oreca second on 1:41.638, about four tenths back, the best of the Dunlop-shod runners. Ben Hanley took the DragonSpeed Oreca #21 third, a further quarter of a second away, even though team-mate Nicolas Lapierre had come to the weekend chasing the outright record for ELMS poles. Norman Nato, making his LMP2 debut, put Racing Engineering fourth on 1:42.130, only eight thousandths ahead of Nelson Panciatici's Duqueine, and Harrison Newey took sixth for APR Rebellion in the #31 Oreca. Orecas set the six fastest laps, and the best Ligier, Will Stevens in the Panis Barthez car, was just over a second off pole in seventh.

Class poles went to David Droux's M.Racing-YMR Norma in LMP3 and Matteo Cairoli's Proton Porsche in GTE, although Gulf Racing's Porsche, second in GTE, had all its times deleted for a non-compliant rear diffuser and was sent to the back of the grid.

chapters.title: Lapierre takes the lead
text: The race started at noon in dry, sunny conditions. Lapierre made the best getaway, passing the TDS Oreca of Francois Perrodo into the first corner and then getting the better of Rojas on the opening lap to lead for DragonSpeed. The pole-sitting IDEC settled in behind. Among the early casualties, Phil Hanson brought the #22 Ligier in after contact with another LMP2 car, which damaged the exhaust and punctured a rear tyre, and the Panis Barthez Ligier, a contender early on, was slowed by a flat tyre. TDS, meanwhile, dropped out of the top ten during its opening stint. After the first round of stops Lapierre still led from Nato, with Pierre Thiriet third in the Signatech Alpine.

chapters.title: Puncture, collision and a safety car
text: DragonSpeed's afternoon turned on a puncture. Lapierre came in with a flat front-left and Henrik Hedman took over, which let Racing Engineering move into the lead shortly before the second round of stops. Nato handed over to Paul Petit after a strong opening stint and the Frenchman built a lead of more than 30 seconds.

That advantage was erased around the halfway mark when Hedman and Duncan Cameron's Spirit of Race Ferrari collided at one of the fast corners and both cars hit the barriers. Neither could continue, and the Full Course Yellow became a Safety Car. The field was neutralised for about 25 minutes and, when the race restarted, Petit led Andre Negrão in the Signatech Alpine, with Panciatici third for Duqueine. Negrão closed right up on Petit and the two fought for the lead with roughly 90 minutes left. Petit held on until the next stops, when Olivier Pla took over for the final stint, while Thiriet took the Alpine back from Negrão and briefly emerged in front of the Racing Engineering car.

chapters.title: Pla wins the duel with Alpine
text: With just under an hour to go Pla caught Thiriet and passed him around the outside at Signes to retake the lead, and from there the Spanish crew pulled away. A splash-and-dash with about 35 minutes left was not enough to undo it, and Pla took the flag 4.827 seconds clear of the #33 TDS Oreca, whose crew avoided a late fuel stop. Behind Thiriet's Alpine, which came under attack from both Vaxiviere and the Duqueine, the fight for the podium went on. Thiriet stayed out longer than his rivals but fell back after his last stop, and Nicolas Jamin passed him with about 25 minutes left to move into third. Jamin finished 7.875 seconds off the winner, just three seconds shy of second.

G-Drive's #26 Oreca, driven in the closing stint by Pizzitola, went past the Alpine for fourth with under 20 minutes to run and finished 11.415 seconds behind, while Thiriet and Negrão's car fell to fifth, almost half a minute back. The second G-Drive car took sixth, and the pole-sitting IDEC was seventh, a lap down. Oreca chassis, including the Alpine-badged car, took the top seven places.

chapters.title: Racing Engineering wins on debut
text: It was a remarkable result for a team new to endurance racing. Racing Engineering won on its ELMS debut with its #24 Oreca, the first overall ELMS wins for Nato and Petit, both making their LMP2 race debuts, and Pla's first since Donington Park in 2012. It was also the team's first win in any category since a Monaco F2 sprint race in 2017. Pla paid tribute to his team-mates, saying Nato had impressed in his first race at the circuit and Petit had coped well with a lot of pressure. Team owner Prince Alfonso de Borbón said he was almost sorry the DragonSpeed car had crashed out, because he felt it would have been a superb battle, and he promised a big season to come.

Hedman, whose collision ended DragonSpeed's race, said afterwards that he had expected the Ferrari to be far enough ahead to take Signes at full speed, committed to the inside and was hit in the side door. He added that he did not think the Ferrari driver had seen him and that it was not deliberate. DragonSpeed's #21 completed only 62 laps and was not classified, as was the Ferrari after 54.

For the two WEC-bound entries the weekend was useful preparation for the new Super Season and Le Mans, and both left with strong results, TDS second and Signatech Alpine fifth. TDS boss Xavier Combet said the plan to share the car among Duval, Perrodo and Vaxiviere in the first three ELMS rounds had come from the drivers, as a way to help Bronze-rated Perrodo measure himself against rivals of similar rating. IDEC Sport had to be content with seventh after leading the way in qualifying, and Duqueine completed the podium. Racing Engineering left Paul Ricard at the top of the LMP2 standings.
The next round of the European Le Mans Series is the 4 Hours of Monza on 13 May, where TDS Racing will once again be on the entry.

facts.v: Chatin took pole with a 1:41.194 in IDEC Sport's brand-new #28 Oreca, four tenths clear of the next LMP2 car, after a red flag halved the ten-minute session.
